subtopics.title: Probability of a union
subtopics.exposition: The sample space contains all possible outcomes of an experiment. P(S) = 1: the probability of observing an outcome from the sample space is 1. The probability of the union of two events is P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B). To get the probability of an event, divide the size of the event by the size of the sample space: P(event) = n(event)/n(S). To use the identity for P(A∪B), first write down the probabilities of the two events, their union and their intersection, each as the number of outcomes in the event divided by n(S); then add P(A) and P(B) and subtract P(A∩B). n(S) denotes the size of the sample space; for the two rolled dice in the example, n(S) = 36.

subtopics.title: Verify the union identity
subtopics.exposition: To find the probabilities from a Venn diagram, count the number of outcomes in each event (A, B, A∩B and A∪B) from the diagram, then divide each count by n(S). To check the identity numerically, substitute the probabilities and calculate P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) = 5/36 + 11/36 − 2/36 = 5/36 + 9/36 = 14/36, then compare with P(A∪B) = 14/36; the two sides are equal, so the identity holds for the example. The identity P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) is proved using Venn diagrams. To prove the identity with Venn diagrams, draw the Venn diagram for each of the 4 terms in the union and intersection identity, then add and subtract the different diagrams. The Venn-diagram proof is carried out for the first column of the Venn diagram figure, and the student should also try it for the other columns. In the Venn-diagram proof, P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) is written as a diagram plus a bracket containing one diagram minus another, which simplifies to one diagram plus another diagram, then to a single diagram, which is P(A∪B). In these Venn diagrams, the area of a region represents its probability.

subtopics.title: Probability of an intersection
subtopics.exposition: The probability of the intersection of two events is the number of outcomes in the intersection divided by the size of the sample space: P(A∩B) = n(A∩B)/n(S); in the example P(A∩B) = 2/36.
